                    1   I.       INTRODUCTION

                    2            Defendants FTI Consulting, Inc. and FTI, LLC (collectively, “FTI”) have conducted

                    3   extensive business in California, benefiting from the forum’s laws and economy for over a decade.

                    4   This dispute, which centers on FTI’s employment of Mr. Poer in its San Francisco, California

                    5   office, on behalf of which he served predominantly California clients, obviously arises from and

                    6   relates to FTI’s California contacts. Yet FTI argues that it is not subject to the jurisdiction of this

                    7   Court and that this is not a proper venue for Mr. Poer’s claims. This is an obvious attempt by FTI

                    8   to reap the benefits of doing business in California, while skirting the State’s worker protection

                    9   laws, which Mr. Poer seeks to enforce. California courts have categorically rejected attempts to

                   10   deny employees the protections of this State on jurisdictional grounds where employers, like FTI,

                   11   have employed the plaintiff employee, have held out that employee to the public as a California

                   12   employee, and have had that employee regularly service numerous California-based clients. FTI’s

                   13   employment of Mr. Poer in California easily satisfies the requirements for personal jurisdiction and

                   14   venue.

                   15            FTI’s attempts to foreclose California protections to Mr. Poer, who worked on behalf of

                   16   FTI in California and now seeks to work for another employer’s California office, is nothing more

                   17   than gamesmanship and forum shopping. Last month, Judge Spero addressed a motion filed by

                   18   FTI against another former employee of their San Francisco office against whom FTI is seeking to

                   19   unlawfully enforce non-compete covenants. As here, FTI alleged that because the plaintiff had

                   20   worked for the San Francisco office remotely from another state in recent years his claims had no

                   21   connection to FTI’s contacts with this forum and that venue was improper. Judge Spero denied

                   22   FTI’s motion, describing his finding of personal jurisdiction was not “even close” and stating FTI’s

                   23   arguments as to venue were “not well taken.” Declaration of Morgan Lewis (“Lewis Decl.”) Ex. 1

                   24   (Westerman v. FTI Consulting, Inc., No. 3:24-CV-04118-JCS, Sept. 5, 2024 Hr’g Tr., at 8:25-

                   18             Mr. Poer easily establishes personal jurisdiction over FTI and readily demonstrates that

                   19   venue is proper in this Court. As to specific personal jurisdiction, FTI hired Mr. Poer to work for

                   20   its San Francisco office and to build and support its California business, which he did by primarily

                   21   serving California clients for over a decade. Moreover, FTI now seeks to prevent him from

                   22   contacting or working with those same California clients. As to venue, a substantial portion of

                   23   events giving rise to this dispute occurred in this District. FTI cannot sidestep California law by

                   24   relying on incidental communications or attendant work that Mr. Poer performed in states other

                   25   than California. There is no jurisdiction or venue more appropriate to preside over this case than

                   26   the Northern District of California.

                    1           A.      FTI Is Subject to Specific Personal Jurisdiction in This District.

1    I.      INTRODUCTION
2            Plaintiff Eric Poer, a remote-work employee in Nevada since 2019,
3    improperly seeks to use California courts to evade his contractual obligations to
4    Defendants FTI Consulting, Inc. and FTI, LLC. FTI maintains that no actual
5    support for the Motion for Preliminary Injunction (“MPI”) exists, and, once tested,
6    Plaintiff’s self-serving declaration will prove lacking. Accordingly, FTI moved for
7    limited expedited discovery (the “Motion”) prior to opposing Plaintiff’s high-stakes
8    MPI so that it could sufficiently defend against it.
9            Plaintiff’s Opposition to FTI’s Motion underscores the need for this basic
10   discovery. Plaintiff continues to tout California’s interest in protecting California
11   employees (despite conceding his Nevada residency) as a basis for denying FTI’s
12   Motion. In doing so, he avoids addressing serious questions regarding California’s
